reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

summary: Fraud detection and credit modelling are decades old; generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 41.0% of firms in Finance and insurance (NAICS 52) answered yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, against a prior period figure of 36.5%. The question was first asked in September 2023, and the survey notes that S means suppressed. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it covers finance and insurance together rather than banking alone.

On what the technology is used for, this site's own coverage says fraud detection and credit models are decades old, while generative AI in service and compliance is the new frontier. Evident Insights, which runs the Evident AI Banking Index, describes itself as an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services, and says banks are among the businesses racing to incorporate the technology into almost everything they do. Evident also writes that several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths, and that AI is breathing new life into Wall Street's tech hiring scene, though landing a software job in finance is shaping up to be more challenging than in recent years.

The benchmark itself is the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard, according to this site's curated points. Evident says the index scores the major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics covering talent, innovation, leadership and transparency, that it launched in January 2023, and that the 2026 Evident AI Index for Banks returns in October. Evident also publishes regional and adjacent indexes, including for banks in Latin America, for banks in the Middle East and Africa, and for insurance, and its Banking Brief newsletter reports over 15,000 subscribers across banking, tech, consulting, academia and government. Evident's CEO, Alexandra Mousavizadeh, is described as a regular commentator on global AI trends.

On the model supply side, this site's Financial Models section tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing licence, downloads and release date, refreshed daily. The page states its source is the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, and carries a last verified date of 2026-10-02.

The regulatory posture is unusual in that it predates the current wave. This site's curated point states that credit and AML models operate under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, making banking the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade, and that the letter is listed in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index. The harvested text from the Federal Reserve page shows a 2011 supervisory letter about prior notices for dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies, so the excerpt itself does not display the SR 11-7 content.

Treasury is cited here as having mapped the risk surface, with a curated point describing a Treasury report on AI in financial services, its uses, opportunities and risks, as framing the US supervisory conversation. The harvested text from the Treasury page, however, concerns OFAC sanctions on 28 individuals and businesses in a global gold smuggling and money laundering network, so the excerpts do not show the AI report's contents. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow reading: adoption in finance and insurance is measured and rising, a public benchmarking index exists for large banks, open financial models are catalogued and tracked, and model risk supervision is the established frame. The sources here do not report ROI evidence, and where they are silent this analysis stays silent too.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The World of AI catalogues the 1,000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each one's licence, download count and release date, and says the list is refreshed daily. The site states that the entries come from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. It gives a last-verified date of 30 September 2026. The page adds that its other sections ,  among them state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary and a tools directory ,  are rebuilt daily from primary sources and carry the date each was last verified.
